note: All data, names and figures are FICTIONAL. Not real market data, not investment advice.

cards.title: Audit before you analyse
cards.what: A data audit is a quick first look at a file: how many rows, which columns, what is blank, what repeats, what looks odd. It tells you whether the numbers can be trusted before you build anything on them.
cards.when_to_use: Every time you open a new file, before any chart or total.
common_mistakes: Jumping straight to a total or chart and trusting it
Only looking at the first few rows
Fixing things silently without writing down what you changed
cards.example: A sales file has 120 rows but only 3 distinct dates for a 7-day week. That gap is a finding: either the export is truncated or days are missing.
cards.how_in_game: Open the file in the Sheet, check the row count, sort each column, and look at the preview before adding any step.

cards.title: Duplicate rows
cards.what: A duplicate is the same record appearing more than once, often because an export was run twice. If you add up duplicated rows, totals come out too big.
cards.when_to_use: When row counts look high, or the same ID, date and amount appear together twice.
common_mistakes: Removing rows that only look alike but are genuine repeat purchases
Deduplicating on one column when the real key is several columns
Forgetting to deduplicate before summing
cards.example: Order 1041, 3 units, 2 March appears twice. The raw total is 40 units, but one of those rows is a copy, so the true total is 37.
cards.how_in_game: Use the Remove duplicates step and pick the key columns (for example order_id plus date). Check the row count before and after.

cards.title: Missing values
cards.what: A missing value is a cell with no information: blank, N/A, null or a placeholder. You can drop the row, fill it with a reasonable value, or leave it out of the calculation, but you must choose on purpose.
cards.when_to_use: When a column has blanks or placeholders such as N/A or a dash.
common_mistakes: Filling with the average without asking why it is missing
Dropping so many rows that the sample becomes biased
Not noticing that different spellings (blank, N/A, none) mean the same thing
cards.example: Prices for 4 of 20 shops are blank. Dropping them leaves 16 shops, but if the blanks are all the cheapest shop type, the average price is now too high.
cards.how_in_game: Use Handle missing: drop, fill with a value, fill with median, or fill with previous value. Look at the preview first.

cards.title: Zero is not the same as missing
cards.what: A real zero means something was measured and the answer was none. A missing value means nobody measured it. Exports often write 0 when the data is simply absent.
cards.when_to_use: When a numeric column suddenly shows many zeros, especially on one day or one region.
common_mistakes: Averaging the fake zeros and dragging the mean down
Treating every zero as an error, even real zero sales
Not asking the data owner what a zero means
cards.example: A shop reports units of 12, 15, 0, 14. If the 0 means the till was offline, the average is 13.7 units over the three good days, not 10.25 over four.
cards.how_in_game: Filter the zeros, compare them with neighbouring rows and other sources, then use Handle missing to treat them as blanks if they are not real.

cards.title: Units and currency
cards.what: A column can mix units: thousands and millions, kilograms and grams, local money and dollars. Numbers are only comparable after you convert them to one unit.
cards.when_to_use: When values in one column differ by factors of 10, 100 or 1000, or when a unit or currency column has more than one value.
common_mistakes: Converting only some rows
Using today's exchange rate for old rows without saying so
Mixing percent (12) with fractions (0.12)
cards.example: Revenue shows 2.5 (in millions) next to 2,400,000 (in plain units). Both are about the same size. Convert both to millions before adding.
cards.how_in_game: Use Convert unit/currency, then Add computed column to apply the factor to the rows that need it. Check the unit column afterwards.

cards.title: Dates and time zones
cards.what: Dates arrive in many formats and time zones. 03/04 may be 3 April or 4 March, and a late-evening sale in one time zone is already tomorrow in another.
cards.when_to_use: When a date column has more than one pattern, or day totals look odd around midnight.
common_mistakes: Guessing the day and month order
Ignoring time zones when comparing two sources
Sorting dates as text so that 10 Mar comes before 2 Mar
cards.example: A row reads 05/06/2026. If other rows read 25/06/2026, the format is day first, so this one is 5 June.
cards.how_in_game: Use Parse date, tell it the format, then sort by the parsed date. Check the earliest and latest dates.

cards.title: Standardise text categories
cards.what: The same category can be typed many ways: Hanoi, Ha Noi, hanoi. A group-by treats each spelling as a separate group, which splits one real group into pieces.
cards.when_to_use: Before grouping or counting by a text column.
common_mistakes: Merging two categories that really are different
Fixing the top spelling but leaving rare ones
Forgetting extra spaces and capital letters
cards.example: Hanoi has 40 units, Ha Noi has 30 and hanoi has 10. The real total for Hanoi is 80, which may change which region ranks first.
cards.how_in_game: Use Standardize text to merge variants. Group by the column and read the list of groups to spot leftovers.

cards.title: Mean versus median
cards.what: The mean adds everything and divides by the count. The median is the middle value when sorted. One huge value drags the mean a lot but barely moves the median.
cards.when_to_use: Whenever you summarise a column that might have extreme values, such as prices, incomes or delivery times.
common_mistakes: Reporting the mean of a very skewed column
Forgetting to say which one you used
Assuming mean and median are close
cards.example: Five salaries: 30, 32, 35, 36, 300. The mean is 86.6 and the median is 35. The median describes the typical person better here.
cards.how_in_game: In Group by + aggregate, choose median as well as mean and compare. A big gap is a warning sign.

cards.title: Outliers and the IQR rule
cards.what: An outlier is a value far from the rest. A common rule: sort the data, find Q1 (the 25% mark) and Q3 (the 75% mark), and call a value an outlier if it is below Q1 - 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR, where IQR = Q3 - Q1. The rule only flags values; you decide what they are.
cards.when_to_use: To find values worth a closer look before taking averages or drawing charts.
common_mistakes: Deleting every flagged value automatically
Applying the rule to naturally skewed data without checking
Running the rule on a tiny sample
cards.example: Values: 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 90. Q1 is 11.5, Q3 is 15.5 (medians of the lower and upper halves), IQR is 4, so the upper fence is 15.5 + 6 = 21.5. Only 90 is flagged.
cards.how_in_game: Use Flag outliers with the IQR rule and read the preview. Then decide: fix, remove or keep.

cards.title: Entry error or real spike?
cards.what: A strange value is either a typing mistake or a real event. Entry errors are usually isolated, off by a clean factor (an extra zero), and not confirmed elsewhere. Real spikes persist, show up in related columns or other sources, and have a story.
cards.when_to_use: When a value is far above or below its neighbours.
common_mistakes: Deleting real events because they look odd
Keeping obvious typos and letting them wreck the average
Not checking a second source
cards.example: Steel price over 6 days: 150, 151, 1520, 152, 153, 152. The jump lasts one day and is exactly 10 times the neighbours: likely an extra zero. A move to 170 that stays at 170 for days is more likely real.
cards.how_in_game: Chart the series as a line, then check neighbours, a second source or the news. Fix the typo, keep the real change.

cards.title: Test and internal accounts
cards.what: Staff and test accounts use the product but are not real customers. They can inflate counts or create fake behaviour such as dozens of tiny purchases.
cards.when_to_use: When user lists contain names like test, demo or admin, or a few IDs show huge activity.
common_mistakes: Leaving test users in conversion numbers
Removing a real power user because they look unusual
Not documenting the rule used to exclude them
cards.example: 12 of 500 signups come from test_01 to test_12. Without them there are 488 real signups, and the conversion rate changes.
cards.how_in_game: Use Filter on the user column, check the preview count, and note the rule in your report.

cards.title: Headers and total rows inside data
cards.what: Some exports repeat the header line or include subtotal and grand-total rows in the middle of the data. If you sum the whole column, these rows are counted twice.
cards.when_to_use: When a column sum looks about double what you expect, or text appears in a number column.
common_mistakes: Summing a column that includes a Total row
Leaving repeated header rows that turn numbers into text
Removing a row that is a real category named Total
cards.example: Rows: A 10, B 20, Total 30. A sum of all three is 60, but the real total is 30.
cards.how_in_game: Use Filter to remove rows where a key column equals Total or repeats the header text.

cards.title: Late-arriving data
cards.what: The most recent day or hour is often incomplete because records are still arriving. Comparing a partial day with full days makes things look like they dropped.
cards.when_to_use: When the last period is much lower than the others or the export time is earlier than the end of the period.
common_mistakes: Reading the last partial day as a real drop
Averaging a partial day with full days
Not checking the export timestamp
cards.example: Sales per day: 100, 104, 98, 102, then 31 at 10:00 on the last day. The 31 is a half-built day, not a crash.
cards.how_in_game: Check the export time, then Filter out the incomplete period or label it as partial in your chart.

cards.title: Join keys that do not match
cards.what: A join links two tables on a shared key, like customer_id. If the keys differ in format or are missing in one table, rows silently disappear or multiply.
cards.when_to_use: Whenever you combine two tables.
common_mistakes: Not checking how many rows matched
Joining on a name instead of an ID
Ignoring leading zeros or extra spaces in keys
cards.example: Table A has ID 007 and table B has 7. The join finds no match for that customer, and the customer vanishes from the result.
cards.how_in_game: Use Lookup/join, then compare the row count to the original and look for blanks in the new columns.

cards.title: Truncated exports
cards.what: A truncated export stops early, often at a round number of rows or at a size limit. Everything after the cut is missing, and the file may not tell you.
cards.when_to_use: When the row count is suspiciously round (1000, 65536) or the data stops in the middle of a period.
common_mistakes: Assuming the file is complete
Analysing only the earlier part and presenting it as the whole
Not asking for a fresh export
cards.example: A year of orders ends on 14 September with exactly 10,000 rows. The cut happened at the limit, so the rest of the year is missing.
cards.how_in_game: Sort by date, look at the last rows and the count, and flag the gap in your findings.

cards.title: Refunds and cancellations
cards.what: Negative amounts are often refunds, which are real events that reduce revenue. Cancelled orders are orders that never completed. They are different things and need different handling.
cards.when_to_use: When a money column has negative values or a status column has cancelled.
common_mistakes: Dropping negative rows and overstating revenue
Counting cancelled orders as sales
Treating a refund as a data error
cards.example: Sales of 100 and 80, then a refund of -30. Net revenue is 150, not 180.
cards.how_in_game: Filter by status for cancellations; keep negative amounts when you want net revenue. Say which one you report.

cards.title: Double counting
cards.what: Double counting means the same thing is included twice, through duplicate rows, overlapping groups or a subtotal added to its parts. It makes totals and percentages too big.
cards.when_to_use: When parts add up to more than the whole, or when merging overlapping lists.
common_mistakes: Adding up groups that overlap, such as users in two segments
Adding subtotals to the rows they summarise
Counting the same customer from two systems
cards.example: A shop has 60 web customers and 50 app customers, but 20 use both. Unique customers are 90, not 110.
cards.how_in_game: Count unique IDs with Remove duplicates and Group by count. Compare the parts to the total.

cards.title: Choosing a chart
cards.what: Match the chart to the question. Line for change over time, bar for comparing categories, scatter for the link between two numbers, histogram for how values are spread.
cards.when_to_use: Before you build any chart.
common_mistakes: Using pie for many slices
Using a line for unordered categories
Choosing a chart because it looks fancy
cards.example: Question: which of 3 regions sold most? Use a sorted bar chart. Question: how did price change over 30 days? Use a line.
cards.how_in_game: In Chart builder, pick the type that fits the question and set a clear axis title with units.

cards.title: Bar charts start at zero
cards.what: A bar's length stands for its value, so the axis must start at zero. If it starts higher, small differences look huge.
cards.when_to_use: Whenever you make a bar chart.
common_mistakes: Cutting the axis to make a change look dramatic
Not labelling the axis
Leaving bars in random order
cards.example: Sales of 98 and 102 on a chart that starts at 96 make one bar look three times as tall as the other. On a zero axis they look nearly equal, which is the truth.
cards.how_in_game: In Chart builder, keep the Y-axis minimum at zero for bars. The quality checker will warn if you truncate it.

cards.title: Line charts for time
cards.what: A line chart connects points in time order, so you can see trend, jumps and seasonality. Time goes left to right, with equal spacing.
cards.when_to_use: To show how a measure changes over days, weeks or months.
common_mistakes: Connecting points that are not in time order
Smoothing so much that real spikes vanish
Skipping missing days without showing the gap
cards.example: Weekly sales: 100, 105, 98, 160, 102. The line shows a one-week spike at 160 that an overall average would hide.
cards.how_in_game: Group by date, then use Chart builder with the date on X and the measure on Y.

cards.title: Scatter plots
cards.what: A scatter plot puts one number on each axis, one dot per item, to show whether two measures move together. It shows association, not cause.
cards.when_to_use: To explore the link between two numeric columns.
common_mistakes: Concluding that one causes the other
Ignoring a few extreme dots that create the pattern
Plotting too many dots on top of each other
cards.example: Across 12 cities, ice cream sales and sunburn cases rise together. A scatter shows the pattern, but hot weather drives both.
cards.how_in_game: Chart builder, scatter type, choose X and Y. Check for outliers before reading the pattern.

cards.title: Histograms
cards.what: A histogram groups values into ranges and shows how many fall in each. It reveals the shape of the data: tight, skewed or with two humps.
cards.when_to_use: To see how a column is spread before deciding between mean and median.
common_mistakes: Using too few or too many bins
Confusing it with a bar chart of categories
Forgetting the vertical axis is a count
cards.example: Delivery times with two humps, one near 2 days and one near 9 days, suggest two different processes mixed together.
cards.how_in_game: Chart builder, histogram, pick the column and try two bin widths.

cards.title: Dual axes and misleading scales
cards.what: A dual-axis chart puts two different scales on one picture. By choosing the scales you can make any two lines look closely linked or completely different.
cards.when_to_use: Rarely. Prefer two small charts side by side.
common_mistakes: Picking scales so the lines line up
Not labelling which axis belongs to which line
Reading a link from the picture alone
cards.example: Sales (0 to 1000) and ad spend (0 to 5) drawn on separate axes can look like twins even if they are unrelated.
cards.how_in_game: Use two charts, or index both to 100 at the start. The quality checker flags dual-axis use.

cards.title: Pie charts: use with care
cards.what: A pie shows parts of one whole, but people judge angles poorly. With many slices or similar sizes, a sorted bar chart is clearer.
cards.when_to_use: Only for two or three parts of a whole that adds to 100%.
common_mistakes: Using a pie for more than five slices
Using a pie for things that do not add to a whole
Adding 3D effects
cards.example: Five regions with shares of 22%, 21%, 20%, 19% and 18% are hard to rank in a pie but easy in a sorted bar.
cards.how_in_game: Choose bar instead of pie in Chart builder unless there are just two or three parts.

cards.title: Sort, label, and give units
cards.what: A clear chart has a title that states the point, labelled axes with units, bars sorted by size when order does not matter, and a source note. A reader should not have to guess.
cards.when_to_use: On every chart that goes into a report.
common_mistakes: Leaving units off the axis
Sorting alphabetically so nobody can rank
Using a title like Chart 1
cards.example: Title: Hanoi sold 120 units, the most of three regions (units per week). That tells the reader the point.
cards.how_in_game: Set title, axis labels and sort in Chart builder. The checker warns about missing units.

cards.title: Moving averages
cards.what: A moving average replaces each point by the average of the last few points. It smooths noise so a trend is easier to see, but it also blurs sudden jumps.
cards.when_to_use: To see the underlying trend in a noisy daily series.
common_mistakes: Using a window so wide that real spikes disappear
Forgetting that the first few points have no full window
Treating the smoothed line as the raw data
cards.example: Daily sales 10, 14, 9, 13, 10, 14, 9. The 3-day average stays between 11 and 12, showing no real trend.
cards.how_in_game: Add computed column, choose moving average with a window of 3 or 7, and chart both lines.

cards.title: Small samples are noisy
cards.what: With few observations, random chance can produce big swings. A 50% rate from 4 users is far less reliable than 50% from 4,000 users.
cards.when_to_use: Any time you compare rates or averages from small groups.
common_mistakes: Celebrating a big change from a handful of cases
Ranking small groups against large ones
Not showing how many cases each number is based on
cards.example: Shop A: 2 of 3 customers returned (67%). Shop B: 600 of 1,000 returned (60%). Shop A is not clearly better; its number is shaky.
cards.how_in_game: Always add a count column next to a rate. Treat groups below about 30 cases with caution.

cards.title: What a p-value means
cards.what: A p-value answers: if there were really no difference, how often would random luck alone produce a gap at least this big? A small p-value (below 0.05 by common convention) means luck is an unlikely explanation. It does not tell you the chance that you are right, or how large or important the effect is.
cards.when_to_use: When comparing two groups, as in an A/B test.
common_mistakes: Saying p = 0.04 means a 96% chance the change works
Treating p = 0.06 as proof of no effect
Ignoring the size of the effect
Testing many things and reporting only the significant one
cards.example: Variant A converts 20 of 200 users (10%). Variant B converts 34 of 200 (17%). The two-sided p-value is about 0.04, so a gap this big would be uncommon if there were no real difference.
cards.how_in_game: Check the test result panel for p and the count per variant. Report both the gap and whether it is significant.

cards.title: Confidence intervals
cards.what: A 95% confidence interval is a range built by a method that, over many repeated studies, captures the true value about 95% of the time. A wide interval means you are uncertain.
cards.when_to_use: To show how precise an estimate is, not just a single number.
common_mistakes: Saying there is a 95% chance the true value is inside this one range
Ignoring a very wide range
Comparing intervals only by eye
cards.example: A conversion rate of 10% from 100 users has a 95% interval of roughly 5% to 18%. From 10,000 users it is roughly 9.4% to 10.6%.
cards.how_in_game: When the report shows a rate, add a count and mention the range if the sample is small.

cards.title: How many users do you need?
cards.what: Before a test, decide the smallest change you care about and how sure you want to be. Smaller changes need many more users. A test that is too small will often miss real effects.
cards.when_to_use: Before running or trusting an A/B test.
common_mistakes: Stopping when the numbers look good
Expecting a tiny change to show up with a few hundred users
Forgetting that the sample is needed per group
cards.example: To detect a rise from 10% to 12% with 80% power at the 5% significance level, you need roughly 3,800 users per variant.
cards.how_in_game: Compare the users per variant in the log with the size suggested in the case hint. If you are short, say the test is underpowered.

cards.title: A/B tests in a nutshell
cards.what: In an A/B test, users are randomly split into groups, each sees a different version, and you compare an outcome such as conversion. Random assignment is what lets you say the version caused the difference.
cards.when_to_use: To decide between two versions of something.
common_mistakes: Comparing groups that were not randomly assigned
Changing several things at once
Looking only at the winner and ignoring group sizes
cards.example: A: 20 of 200 (10%). B: 34 of 200 (17%). The gap is 7 points. Check that the groups are about equal size and that p is small.
cards.how_in_game: Group by variant, count users, compute conversion, then read the significance check.

cards.title: Peeking at A/B tests
cards.what: If you check a running test again and again and stop the first time p is below 0.05, you will find false winners far more often than 5%. With ten looks the false alarm rate is closer to one in five.
cards.when_to_use: When someone asks to stop a test early because it looks good.
common_mistakes: Stopping on the first significant result
Extending the test only when the result is disappointing
Not fixing the sample size in advance
cards.example: A test with no real difference is checked 10 times. Roughly 1 in 5 such tests will show p below 0.05 at some look.
cards.how_in_game: Set the sample size first and read the result once at the end, or treat early reads as provisional.

cards.title: Seasonality versus trend
cards.what: Seasonality is a repeating pattern, such as weekend peaks or December sales. A trend is a steady change in the level. Comparing a seasonal peak with an off-season month can look like growth when it is only the calendar.
cards.when_to_use: When comparing periods in a time series.
common_mistakes: Comparing December with January and calling it a crash
Comparing with the previous month instead of the same month last year
Fitting a straight line through a seasonal pattern
cards.example: Sales are 150 in December and 100 in January every year. This January against last January is the fair comparison.
cards.how_in_game: Line chart with several years overlaid, or compare to the same period last year using Add computed column.

cards.title: Base rates
cards.what: The base rate is how common something is to begin with. When the thing is rare, even an accurate alarm gives mostly false alarms.
cards.when_to_use: When a test, alert or flag points at a rare event.
common_mistakes: Ignoring how rare the event is
Reading a 90% accurate flag as a 90% chance
Not counting false alarms
cards.example: Fraud affects 1% of 1,000 payments, so 10 are fraud. The alarm catches 9 of them and falsely flags 99 of the 990 honest ones. Of 108 flags, only 9 (about 8%) are real fraud.
cards.how_in_game: Build a small table: total, real cases, flagged real, flagged false. Use Group by count.

cards.title: Regression to the mean
cards.what: Extremely high or low results tend to be followed by more average ones, because extreme values contain a lot of luck. A fix applied right after a terrible week can look effective when nothing changed.
cards.when_to_use: When you pick the worst or best performers and measure again.
common_mistakes: Crediting a fix for a natural bounce-back
Rewarding or blaming people for random swings
Selecting extremes and comparing them without a control group
cards.example: The 5 shops with the lowest sales last month improve by 8% this month without any action, because last month included bad luck.
cards.how_in_game: Chart several periods, not one. Compare treated shops with similar untreated shops.

cards.title: Percent versus percentage points
cards.what: A change from 10% to 12% is 2 percentage points but a 20% relative increase. Both are true, but they sound very different, so always say which one you mean.
cards.when_to_use: Whenever you describe a change in a rate.
common_mistakes: Saying the rate rose 2% when you mean 2 points
Hiding a tiny absolute change behind a large relative one
Averaging percentages without weights
cards.example: Conversion goes from 5.0% to 5.5%: +0.5 points, or +10% relative.
cards.how_in_game: Use Add computed column for both the difference and the ratio, and label them clearly.

cards.title: Correlation is not causation
cards.what: Two things moving together does not mean one causes the other. A third factor may drive both, the link may be chance, or the cause may run the other way.
cards.when_to_use: Whenever you see two measures that rise or fall together.
common_mistakes: Announcing a cause from a chart
Ignoring a hidden third factor
Assuming that the order of events proves the cause
cards.example: Across 12 cities, those with 2x the ice cream sales have more sunburn. Sunshine drives both; banning ice cream will not cure sunburn.
cards.how_in_game: Use a scatter to see the link, then look for a third factor by splitting with Group by. Word findings as 'is associated with'.

cards.title: Confounders
cards.what: A confounder is a third factor that affects both the thing you change and the outcome, creating a false or distorted link. Random assignment in a test removes most confounding.
cards.when_to_use: When groups differ in more than the thing you are studying.
common_mistakes: Comparing groups that differ in age, region or device mix
Not checking group makeup
Assuming adjustment fixes everything
cards.example: App users spend 35 per order versus 20 for others, but they are also younger and richer. The app may not be the reason.
cards.how_in_game: Split by the suspected factor with Group by and compare like with like.

cards.title: Simpson's paradox
cards.what: Sometimes one option wins inside every subgroup but loses overall, because the groups are mixed in different proportions. Always check whether a split changes the story.
cards.when_to_use: When overall results and subgroup results seem to disagree, or when groups have very different sizes.
common_mistakes: Trusting the overall total without splitting
Always trusting the split without thinking about which one answers your question
Not checking how the groups are weighted
cards.example: Variant A: 160 of 800 desktop (20%), 8 of 200 mobile (4%), total 16.8%. Variant B: 44 of 200 desktop (22%), 40 of 800 mobile (5%), total 8.4%. B wins on both devices but loses overall, because B got mostly mobile users.
cards.how_in_game: Group by variant and by device, then compare rates within each device.

cards.title: Survivorship bias
cards.what: Survivorship bias happens when you only look at what survived, so failures are missing from the data. The picture is too rosy.
cards.when_to_use: When a dataset only lists active, open or successful items.
common_mistakes: Studying only current customers to explain churn
Judging a strategy only by its winners
Not asking what was filtered out before you got the file
cards.example: A loan book lists only open accounts. Defaulted accounts were removed, so the default rate looks like 0%.
cards.how_in_game: Ask what is missing, look for status columns, and request the closed records if you can.

cards.title: Cherry-picking
cards.what: Cherry-picking means showing only the data points that support a story, such as a lucky date range. The facts are real but the picture is false.
cards.when_to_use: When someone gives you a time window or subset you did not choose.
common_mistakes: Choosing start and end dates to get the trend you want
Reporting the best of many tests
Leaving out the periods that disagree
cards.example: Sales are up 30% from a weak Tuesday to a strong Friday, yet down 5% over the full month.
cards.how_in_game: Chart the full range and say why any window was chosen before you saw the result.

cards.title: Funnel analysis
cards.what: A funnel counts how many users reach each step of a journey, for example visit, sign-up, purchase. The step with the biggest proportional drop is the first place to look for a problem.
cards.when_to_use: To find where users give up in a process.
common_mistakes: Comparing step drops in raw numbers instead of percentages
Mixing users from different days into one step
Ignoring an incomplete last day
cards.example: 1,000 visit, 300 start sign-up, 240 finish, 60 buy. Step rates: 30%, 80%, 25%. The weakest step after the first is finish to buy (25%).
cards.how_in_game: Group by step, compute the rate from each step to the next, and chart as a sorted bar.

cards.title: Cohort retention
cards.what: A cohort is a group of users who started in the same period. Retention is the share of the cohort still active after 1 week, 2 weeks, and so on. It compares like with like, so growth in new users does not hide churn.
cards.when_to_use: To judge whether customers stick around, or whether a change helped retention.
common_mistakes: Mixing old and new users in one retention number
Comparing cohorts of different ages
Forgetting closed accounts
cards.example: Of 200 users who joined in January, 120 were active in week 1 and 80 in week 4. Week-4 retention is 40%.
cards.how_in_game: Add a computed column for start month and weeks since start, then Pivot cohort by week.

cards.title: Segmentation
cards.what: Segmentation splits users into groups that behave differently, such as by region, device or spending. An average over everyone can hide what each segment is doing.
cards.when_to_use: When the average seems to hide something, or when different groups need different actions.
common_mistakes: Making too many tiny segments
Choosing segments after seeing the result to fit a story
Forgetting group sizes
cards.example: Average basket is 20. New customers spend 12 and loyal customers spend 35. One average describes neither group.
cards.how_in_game: Group by the segment column with count and mean, and compare.

cards.title: Root-cause drill-down
cards.what: When a metric changes, split it step by step: by time, region, product, channel. Keep drilling into the part that moved most until you find the source. Then check that the explanation covers the whole change.
cards.when_to_use: When the boss asks why something went up or down.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the first plausible reason
Explaining the change with a story that fits only part of it
Not checking whether the change is really a data issue
cards.example: Revenue fell 10%. Split by region: only Hue fell, by 40%. Split Hue by product: one product was out of stock.
cards.how_in_game: Group by one dimension at a time, compare with the previous period, and chart the biggest changes.

cards.title: Plan the analysis
cards.what: Before touching data, write the question, the metric, the comparison and what result would change your mind. This stops you wandering and fitting a story afterwards.
cards.when_to_use: At the start of any case.
common_mistakes: Starting with a chart and hunting for a story
Using a metric you did not define
Changing the question after seeing the data
cards.example: Question: did sales rise this week? Metric: units per day. Comparison: previous 7 days. Decision: call it a rise if more than 5% higher.
cards.how_in_game: Read the boss question, note the metric and the comparison, then choose the files and steps.

cards.title: Keep an assumptions log
cards.what: An assumptions log is a short list of choices you made, such as 'removed test accounts' or 'treated zeros as missing'. It lets others check your work and explains differences between analysts.
cards.when_to_use: Any time you make a judgement call in cleaning or analysis.
common_mistakes: Making silent fixes
Writing vague notes
Forgetting the assumptions when you set confidence
cards.example: Assumption: the 0 units on 4 March means the till was offline, so it is treated as missing.
cards.how_in_game: The step list in the Sheet is your log. Add a short note in your report for each non-obvious step.

cards.title: Write clear findings
cards.what: A good finding states what you measured, how big the change is, what comparison you used, and how sure you are. Keep it short and avoid claims the data cannot support.
cards.when_to_use: When filling in the report.
common_mistakes: Overstating certainty
Reporting only the number without the comparison
Hiding the limits of the data
cards.example: Weak: Sales are up. Strong: Units are 8% higher than the previous 7 days (310 vs 287), based on 14 stores, after removing duplicate rows.
cards.how_in_game: Pick the findings that match your cleaned table and attach at most three pieces of evidence.

cards.title: Confidence means honesty
cards.what: Confidence is how sure you are, not how bold you sound. Over time, your 70% answers should be right about 70% of the time. Dirty data, small samples and untested assumptions all lower honest confidence.
cards.when_to_use: When you set the confidence level in your report.
common_mistakes: Always choosing high confidence
Always choosing low confidence to be safe
Not lowering confidence when the data was dirty or small
cards.example: You make ten forecasts at 70% confidence and 7 come true: that is well calibrated.
cards.how_in_game: After cleaning, ask: how many rows, how clean, is the test significant? Then set the confidence slider.
